headline: The Race Running 4-Plus Knots: Bonito Push In, Bass Still Sitting on Bait
subhead: Building tides ahead of the full moon are loading up Valiant Rock and Plum Gut while stripers wait for the bunker to bunch.
body_markdown:
Four-point-two knots on the peak ebb through the Race this week, and climbing. That's not a guess — that's what the tide tables are showing as the moon builds toward full on the 6th and 7th, and it's the number that matters most right now for anyone running gear through Valiant Rock or dropping into Plum Gut. Bigger tides mean harder current, harder current means tighter bait, and tighter bait is exactly what this zone has been missing for the last two weeks. The slack windows are getting shorter too — figure a 15 to 20 minute true slack at Valiant Rock on the last of the ebb, usually sliding into early-to-mid afternoon this week, and a similar short window on the front of the flood before the rip builds back up. That's your work zone. Miss it by half an hour either way and you're fighting current that'll sweep a bucktail sideways before it ever gets down.

The bigger regional story is the bonito. They've been stacking at Block Island and Point Judith for weeks, and the push west is now showing up in real numbers — Fishers Island Sound, the eastern approaches to the Race, and pockets around Little Gull and Great Gull Island. Water's cooperating: New London is holding around 69.4°F, Kings Point over in the western Sound is up near 70.9, and that gradient is exactly the kind of setup that funnels bait and predators together as they move down-Sound. The catch is that a lot of these bonito are locked onto micro-bait — bay anchovies, tiny silversides — and they're being fussy about it. Standard 2-ounce metals are getting looked at and refused more than they're getting bit. The boats doing damage are downsizing hard: quarter-ounce and 3/8-ounce epoxy jigs in the Gut, worked on 20-pound fluoro, fast retrieve with a pause. Same story with false albacore mixed into the same schools — they're keying on the same micro-bait, and the small profile stuff is out-fishing anything flashy two or three to one right now.

Striped bass are the tougher conversation. The bass are here, they're just not committed yet. Bunker schools are thickening up in Raritan Bay, the LI south shore, and Narragansett Bay, but the water's still warm enough — low-to-mid 70s in a lot of those staging areas — to keep those schools loose and the bass non-committal instead of blitzing on top. We flagged this exact pattern last week: said the trigger was bait density, and that once those bunker schools tightened up under a building moon, bass would start committing in blitz numbers within a week or two. That hasn't broken yet, but the ingredients are lining up fast, and the full moon this weekend is the next real catalyst. In the meantime, the better bass action in this zone is coming the old-fashioned way — wire line and bucktails worked deep and slow through Valiant Rock and the western edge of Race Rock on the last two hours of the ebb, when the current is still strong enough to hold bait but starting to ease off the boil. Bucktails in the 2 to 4-ounce range, white or olive, tipped with a strip of fresh bunker, dragged just off bottom in 40 to 60 feet. Fish are coming up mixed sizes — some slot, some pushing overslot — but nobody's filling a box in an hour. It's a program, not a blitz, right now.

Bluefish are the one bite in this zone that hasn't needed any qualifiers. They've been consistent through the Race and out toward the Sluiceway, feeding hard on peanut bunker and whatever else gets pushed through the rip on the tide change. We said last week the warm water would keep them aggressive and widespread through Labor Day week, and that's exactly what's happened — jumbo blues mixed in with the bass at Valiant Rock, and smaller choppers stacked thick enough in Plum Gut to keep light-tackle guys busy between albie and bonito runs. Poppers and metal-lip swimmers worked over the rip on the top of the tide are getting hit hard; don't be surprised if wire leader saves you a few rigs.

Black sea bass remain the dependable structure bite while everything else sorts itself out. Drops around Great Gull Island and the rockier stretches off Plum Gut are holding fish on squid strips and Gulp on standard sea bass rigs, 40 to 70 feet. Fluke, on the other hand, are winding down the way they always do in early September — the doormats have mostly abandoned the shallower structure for deeper ocean-side ground, and what's left inside is mostly short fish. Not worth building a whole trip around anymore in this zone.

Looking ahead: the full moon on the 6th and 7th is going to push tidal flow even harder through the Race and Plum Gut, which should tighten up bait further and could be the spark that finally gets the bass moving in earnest — though the more likely first blitz zones are still Raritan Bay or the LI south shore, where bunker density is thickest. If that breaks, expect the ripple effect to reach this zone within days as bass push east along the migration corridor. For the next 48 to 72 hours, the smart play is running the slack windows at Valiant Rock for bass and bluefish, then working the Gut with small profile jigs for bonito and albies on the stronger stages of the tide. Watch the wind — anything out of the southwest holds the bonito pattern together, while a hard northeast blow will stir the rip enough to shut the visual bite down fast.
